Based on the information provided, it appears that the Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the case of Zagham Hassan Khan v. The State, etc., has set aside the order of the Lahore High Court and the trial court, allowing the appeal and ordering the release of the petitioner on bail. The petitioner, who is suffering from schizophrenia and is about 60 years old, was found unfit to stand trial under Section 465 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC). The Supreme Court has directed that the petitioner be released on bail subject to certain conditions, including proper care by a family member and periodic medical examinations.
The Supreme Court's decision to release the petitioner on bail is consistent with the principles enunciated in Section 466, CrPC, which provides for the release of an accused person found to be of unsound mind on sufficient security. The Court emphasized that the primary course prescribed by Section 466, CrPC, is to release the accused on sufficient security, with detention in safe custody being the exception. The Court found that the trial court had unreasonably exercised its discretion in detaining the petitioner in a Mental Health Institute without justifiable reasons, and that the High Court failed to correct this error in its revisional jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court's judgment in this case reflects a humane approach towards individuals with mental disabilities and underscores the importance of proper care and treatment for such individuals within the legal framework. The decision also highlights the Court's role in ensuring that the discretion granted to lower courts under the CrPC is exercised reasonably and in accordance with the law.

Through this order, I intend to dispose of the instant petition filed by the petitioner/respondent for the grant of a temporary injunction. Perusal of the record transpires that the instant suit has been filed against the petitioner/plaintiff for possession through partition and perpetual injunction in respect of suit Khasra No.2933/510, measuring 01-Kanal & 17-Marlas, situated in Moza Derwaish, Tehsil & District Haripur, to the extent of the petitioner's shares, i.e., 01-Kanal & 02-Marlas (9152/15392), or whichever is as per record, further details of which are fully described in the headnote of the plaint. The respondent was summoned, whereupon the respondent appeared before the court and contested the suit by submitting a wakalatnama along with a written reply.
The learned counsel for the petitioner, during the course of arguments, asserted that he has a strong prima facie case; that the balance of convenience lies in favor of the petitioner and that he would suffer irreparable loss if a temporary injunction is not granted. On the contrary, the respondents, through counsel, hotly contested the instant application by filing a written reply on the ground that the suit property is properly partitioned. The petitioners/plaintiffs have a "Plaza" on their own shares, and they have their own construction on their shares, which are also approved by the Municipal Committee Haripur, with which the respondents have no concern. They are owners in Khasra No.508, and the plaintiffs/petitioners have no concern with Khasra No.507. At the end, they requested the dismissal of the instant petition.
Arguments were heard, and the record was perused. For the grant of a temporary injunction, under Order 39, Rule 1 & 2 of the CPC, the three essential ingredients, i.e., prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable loss, must co-exist side by side in favor of a person so claiming, and if any one of these is missing, an injunction cannot be granted. In support of his stance, the petitioner annexed copies of fard jamabandi and Girdawari e Malikiyat, which show the joint ownership of the petitioner. The controversy between the parties is factual in nature, which could only be resolved through recording pro and contra evidence of the parties. It is also well-settled law that to grant a temporary injunction, it is not compulsory for the party to show his/her title. It is sufficient for the petitioner to show that he/she has an arguable case in his/her favor. Moreover, one of the main purposes of granting a temporary injunction is to preserve the subject in controversy. As far as the other two ingredients are concerned, they too tilt in favor of the petitioners in the sense that if a temporary injunction is declined and the suit property is alienated, it will cause inconvenience, multiplicity of litigation, and will create third-party interest in the disputed property. Hence, for the reasons stated above, the application of the petitioner is accepted to the extent of further alienation of disputed shares in the suit property for six months or until the disposal of the instant suit, whichever is earlier. Parties to bear their own costs.
This order is tentative in nature and shall not affect the merits of the case in the long run. A copy of this order shall be placed on the main file, while the instant petition shall be consigned to the record room after its necessary compilation and completion

IN THE COURT OF NADEEM ANWAR CH.ADDL. SESSIONS JUDGE/ JUDGE SPECIAL COURT CNSA, LAHORENarcotics Case No. 60 of 2024Narcotics Trial No. 21978 of 2023The StateVs.Muhammad Imran, S/o Muhammad Shahbaz, Caste Rajput Bhatti, R/o Shezan Factory Near Furniture Market, Band Road, Lahore.	         	  FIR NO.1796 DATED 06.05.2023OFFENCE U/S 9(1) 3c OF CNSA, 1997POLICE STATION NAWAN KOT, LAHOREJUDGMENT:		The brief facts giving rise to registration of FIR No.1796 dated 06.05.2023 for the commission of offence punishable u/s 9(1) 3c of CNSA registered at police station Nawan Kot, Lahore are that on 06.05.2023 Muhammad Arslan Ijaz T/SI alongwith Mukhtar and Nazim constables was present on his routine patrol duty at Yateem Khana Chowk, Lahore. On Spy information, complainant constituted a raiding party and on the pointation of informer, he apprehended the present accused who disclosed his name as Muhammad Imran. On his personal search, Charas weighing 1540-gram was recovered from the blue shopping bag holding in his right hand. Out of the recovered contraband, 77-gram Charas was separated as sample for chemical analysis. The recovered Charas and sample were made into sealed parcels and taken into possession vide recovery memo by the complainant. Complainant drafted complaint and sent the same to police station for registration of formal FIR through Mukhtar constable upon which case FIR No.1796/2023 was registered.2.		On registration of FIR, the case was investigated by Muhammad Aurangzeb S.I, PW-5, who on conclusion of his investigation, having found the accused involved, challaned him for his trial u/s 9(1) 3c of CNSA. The accused was charge sheeted for commission of offence punishable u/s 9(1) 3c of CNSA, 1997 but he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Hence, the prosecution was required to produce its evidence which was concluded as under: PW-1:Abbas Ali ASI(Duty Officer)PW-2:Muhammad Arslan Ijaz T/SI(Complainant)PW-3:Mukhtar 12808/C(Recovery Witness)PW-4:Shahzad Iqbal 1958/HC(Moharar)PW-5:Muhammad Aurangzeb SI(Investigation Officer)PW-6:Ms. Zaigum Ashiq (NAR-3-JFS)(Forensic Scientist)Ex. PA:ComplaintEx. PA/1:F.I.REx. PB:Recovery MemoEx. PC:Rough Site PlanEx. PD:PFSA Report	3.	On conclusion of evidence of prosecution, the accused was examined u/s 342 Cr.P.C, he denied the allegations and professed his innocence. Muhammad Imran, accused neither opted to produce defence evidence nor did opt to appear on oath in terms of section 340(2) Cr. P.C. While replying to the question that why this case has been lodged against him and why the PWs have deposed against him, he stated as under: - “I am innocent. In fact the police called me through my friend at butcher house at 10:00 pm on 05.05.2023 but the police registered the case on 06.05.2023. The police involved me in this case falsely and planted fake recovery against me just to strengthen this false case, in order to show their efficiency. The PWs are the police officials. They have deposed against me being in league with each other, just to strengthen this false case. The case is false and frivolous and just lodged to get money from me and demanded Rs.01-Lac which I could not pay. The informer of police was just like my friend and he involved me out of greed because he often used to come on my shop for refreshment. When he imagined that I could pay handsome amount he got me involved in the false case”4.	Learned ADPP while summing up the case of prosecution argued that the prosecution has succeeded in proving its case against the accused through the testimony of independent and uninterested witnesses beyond shadow of doubt; the time, place and mode of recovery of Charas from the accused have been established by the prosecution witnesses by narrating the whole proceedings in a truthful manner, whereas, the defence awfully failed in surfacing any anomaly creating any considerable dent in the evidence of prosecution witnesses. He further submitted that there is no serious infirmity or material discrepancy in evidence of prosecution witnesses who had no reason to falsely implicate the accused in this case; the positive report of PFSA authenticates that the substance recovered from the accused was Charas as believed by complainant and Investigation Officer. Further added that the accused neither opted to appear in the witness box u/s 340(2) Cr.P.C. nor did he produce defence evidence. Consequently, the prosecution has succeeded in proving its case against the accused beyond shadow of doubt, whereas, the accused could not put forward any plausible explanation that why he was roped in this case falsely. All these aspects make the case of accused quite fit for his conviction for commission of offence charged with.5.	On the other hand, learned defence counsel argued that the prosecution has awfully failed to establish the mode of recovery as alleged by it; the discrepancies in evidence of prosecution witnesses show that they have not deposed truthfully; there are number of material inconsistencies in evidence of prosecution witnesses, which make its story quite implausible and doubtful; the parcel of sample was deposited in the PFSA with inordinate delay, which shows that the case property comprising sample parcel was managed, subsequently. Summing up the arguments, learned defence counsel vehemently prayed for acquittal of the accused standing trial.6.	Arguments heard and record perused.7.	In order to bring home guilt of accused Muhammad Imran in this case, it was for the prosecution to prove its story contained in complaint, Ex.PA and F.I.R, Ex.PA/1 through cogent, tangible and confidence inspiring evidence. For this purpose the prosecution has produced complainant Muhammad Arslan Ijaz T/SI and recovery witness Mukhtar 12808/C as PW-2 & PW-3, respectively. It is pertinent to mention here that the recovery witnesses remained consistent as to time, place and mode of recovery of narcotic substance from the present accused. In cross-examination, the defence failed to shatter their consistency and credibility or to bring on record any material contradiction or serious infirmity. The minor discrepancies are always natural and likewise ignorable. The report of PFSA, Lahore regarding the analysis of narcotics is available on the record as Exh.PD. It is evident from the said report that one (01) sealed sample parcel of suspected Charas weighing 77-gram separated from the recovered Charas of this case was submitted in the office of PFSA, Lahore and on analysis, the net weight of sample was found as 77.46-gram and the material in said sealed sample parcel was found to be containing Charas. In this way, the prosecution version is also fully corroborated by the report of PFSA, Lahore (Exh.PD). 8.	So far as the safe custody and safe transmission of the sample parcel and parcel of remaining case property said to contain Charas, are concerned, it is worth mentioning here that it is proved from the evidence of prosecution witnesses that the sample parcel and parcel of remaining case property said to contain Charas were kept in safe custody and the same were also safely transmitted to the office of PFSA, Lahore and ‘sadar malkhana’, respectively. During investigation, the present accused was found to be fully involved in the occurrence of this case and his name was placed in column No.3 of the report u/s 173 Cr.P.C. There is nothing available on the record to suggest that the investigation of this case was challenged by the present accused before the higher police officers or any other competent forum.9.	Another important aspect of the present case is that during their cross-examination, the complainant Muhammad Arslan Ijaz T/SI (PW-2) stated categorically that recovered Charas was consisted of several pieces and he (PW-2) prepared sample from one piece only. The recovery witness Mukhtar 12808/C (PW-3) also stated in line with the deposition of complainant. Both the witnesses were not able to mention the weight of each piece of recovered Charas, because the pieces of recovered Charas were not separately weighed by the complainant. The testimony of the star witnesses has established the fact of preparing one sample from all recovered pieces of Charas by the complainant. 10.		In view of the above mentioned statements of the said material prosecution witnesses of this case, it is evident that the recovered contraband material was consisting of many pieces and sample was taken from one piece only for chemical analysis. It has not been brought on record that what was the exact weight of each piece of recovered Charas. As only one sample parcel containing 77-gram Charas was obtained from only one piece of the recovered Charas and the same was sent to the office of PFSA, Lahore, therefore, the said sample cannot be considered as a representative sample of the whole contraband material recovered in this case. Reliance in this respect is placed on the judgment passed by the august Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case titled “Ameer Zeb  .Vs.  The State.” reported in PLD 2012 Supreme Court 380. In these circumstances, it can be safely held that the prosecution could not prove its case beyond the shadow of any doubt against the present accused to the extent of recovery of Charas weighing 1540-gram, however, the prosecution has proved its case against the present accused to the extent of recovery of Charas weighing 77-gram which was sent to the office of PFSA, Lahore for chemical analysis, having positive report, Ex.PD. As discussed above, the safe custody and safe transmission of the sample parcel to the office of PFSA is also proved by the prosecution witnesses.11.		Foregoing in view, the accused Muhammad Imran is held guilty for possessing 77-gram Charas and he is accordingly convicted u/s 9(1) 3a of CNSA, 1997 instead of offence u/s 9(1)3c of CNSA, 1997 and sentenced to undergo one year R.I with fine of Rs.20,000/- (Rupees Twenty Thousand only). In case of default in payment of fine, he shall further undergo Two Months S.I. The benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C, is also extended in favour of the convict. The convict Muhammad Imran is present in court in custody. He be sent back to District Jail, Lahore for serving out the sentence awarded to him today. The said convict, present before this Court, is informed that he can file an appeal against this judgment within the prescribed period. The copy of this judgment be supplied to the convict namely Muhammad Imran free of cost. Copy of this judgment be also dispatched to the Officer Incharge of prosecution District Lahore in the light of section 373 Cr.P.C. The case property i.e. recovered Charas, is confiscated in favour of the State and be destroyed as per law and rules after the lapse of period of appeal/revision, if any. IN THE COURT OF ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE-IX, QUETTA.				                     Crl. Bail Application No.06/2024.Aminullah Son of Muhammad Sadiq,Presently confined at District Jail, Quetta.		      Applicant/Accused. 				VERSUS.The State						                Respondent.OFFENCE UNDER SECTION 377, 34 PPC APPLICATION U/S 497 Cr.P.C FOR GRANT OF BAIL.O R D E R.26th February, 2024.1.		This order is meant to dispose of above titled application moved by accused/applicant through counsel Mr. Zahid Agha Advocate in case FIR No.13/2023 registered for offence U/S 377, 34 PPC. The State was represented by Deputy District Public Prosecutor Mr. Khalid Ahmed. 2.		Brief facts of case are as that complainant lodged report at P.S Hanna Urak upon allegation of sodomy with his child of 12/13 years of age. As per report on 18.05.2023 at about 08:45 P.M, his child named Ihsanullah was forcibly taken by accused persons Ihsanullah and Rohullah on their motorcycle nearby hills. Where accused persons Ihsanullah, Rohullah and their other companions, namely, Asmatullah, Noor Ali, Ahmed Ullah, Aminullah and Gulab, already present over there, committed forcibly unnatural offence with minor Ihsanullah. On report of father of child, case was registered. Accused persons were arrested. Instant bail application has been made on behalf of accused Aminullah. 3.		Following the registration of application. Notice to State was issued. 4.		Arguments were heard from both side. Counsel for applicant mainly stressed that case to the extent of applicant/accused Aminullah is of further inquiry as DNA report of applicant/accused did not match. So no convincing evidence to connect applicant/accused with alleged offence is available with prosecution. 5.		Perusal of record shows that accused/applicant was directly nominated in FIR by complainant while victim in his statement U/S 164 Cr.P.C also nominated accused/applicant alongwith other accused persons by assigning each accused a role and participation in alleged commission of offence. 6.		So far as, negative report of DNA to extent of accused/applicant is concerned, same cannot serve as a ground to absolve accused from alleged commission of offence without other relevant and circumstantial evidence. Because perusal of DNA report clearly reads that date of submission of evidence to PFSA is 16th June, 2023, while incident/offence was committed on 18th May, 2023. It implies that sample received to lab were 29 days old. Admittedly, DNA testing can only reliably lead to an offender if the sample is tested within the span of the first 7 days of the commission of offence. So in such position, negative DNA report cannot be considered for grant of bail as offence with which accused is charged falls within prohibitory of Section 497 Cr.P.C and punishable to life imprisonment or to the extent of 10 years. Reliance is placed on following case law.Jai Kumar & others Vs. The StateHigh Court of Sindh Circuit Court, Hyderabad.Wherein, it is held that:-“After indulging in some studies, this Court was made aware that the earlier the samples are collected and tested, the more accurate results it yields. Per numerous studies, DNA testing can only reliably lead to an offender if the sample is tested within the span of the first 7 days of the offence occurring. Conclusively, the DNA report coming in negative is barely of any help to the case of applicant for grant of his bail, especially when the offence with which he is charged falls within the prohibitory clause of S. 497 Cr.P.C and is punishable up to death or life imprisonment. Even otherwise, the effect of the DNA report will be considered during the trial after evaluating the evidence produced by the parties.”7.		Apart from DNA, other evidence as mentioned above is available on record to connect accused/applicant with non-bailable case. Hence, accused/applicant have failed to make out a prima face case within purview of Section 497 (2) Cr.P.C.8.		  In view of observation made hereinabove, I am not inclined to accept the instant application. Same is hereby dismissed, accordingly. 9.		 Needless to add here that the observations, made herein above are purely tentative in nature, which shall not affect the merits of this case. Announced in the open court26th February, 2024.      	          (GHULAM MUSTAFA ROONJHA)          			                           ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE-IX, 							          QUETTA.

IN THE COURT OF AMBREEN BATOOL FATIMA- IIIRD SENIOR CIVIL JUDGE AT SHAHEED BENAZIRABAD 
Civil Execution Application No. 03/2024
First Class Civil Suit No. 137/2022

ORDER
08-03-2025
This order shall dispose off the above captioned civil Execution Application filed by the decree-holders through their counsel for execution of the decree dated 14-02-2024 passed by this Court in the above captioned suit. 
2.	The mode of execution proposed by the decree-holders through the instant application is as under:
This Honourable Court may be pleased to direct the JD no. 01 to pay the rent arrears to the extent of shares to the Decree-Holders with effect from 01-09-2020 till date. Further. That the JD no. 01 and 02 be bound to pay the rent to the extent of the share of the Decree-holders till the shop is partitioned and separate possessions is handed over to the decree-holders. Further that the JD no. 01 and 02 be permanently restrained from collecting/receiving the rent from the tenancies since passing of this judgment  and further be restricted from selling or handing over the possessions or changing the complexion of the suit shop in any manner. 
	3.	Notice of the application was duly served upon the judgment-debtors. JD no. 01 appeared and filed his objections on 07-09-2024, which were taken on record. Whereas JD no. 02 was called absent despite service being held good upon him. Therefore, the Learned Predecessor Judge vide his order dated 17-01-2025, debarred Judgment Debtors no. 02 to 06 and the matter proceeded to Hearing. 
4.	While being heard, the counsel for counsel for decree-holders submitted, inter alia, that the subject decree had attained the finality as the judgment-debtors had not assailed the same, thus the same was very much within the field, thus entitled to be executed in its letter and spirit. On the other hand the Judgment debtor 1 mainly claimed that JD no. 02 was resposible to secure tenants for the shop and as been receiving the shares of the Plaintiffs and that he has only received his share. In other words, he admitted that the shares of the Plaintiffs’ rent is lying with the JD no. 02, who is also the real brother of the JD no. 01 and the Plaintiffs.
5.	Heard and perused. The record reveals that the DHs filed the FC suit no. 72 of 2022 before the Learned Predecessor Judge on 25-02-2022 for declaration, settlement of accounts, Mesne Profits and Injunction under order VII Rule 1 CPC. Perusal of the same file reveals that service was effected through all modes upon the JDs and finally the same was held good by the Learned Predecessor Judge vide order dated 14-07-2022.Thereafter, the JDs failed to appear and submit their written statement, hence they were debarred via order passed by the Learned Predecessor Judge on 10-11-2022 and the matter proceeded ex-parte. After recording of evidence, the learned Predecessor Judge disposed off the matter via exparte Judgment/decree dated 14-02-2024.

6.	There is nothing on record to suggest that any appeal has been preferred against the subject decree and this Court has not received any intimation to that effect. Thus, the said judgment and decree has attained the finality. The objections raised by the JD no. 01 are devoid of force and merit. The JD no. 01 in fact admitted that JD no. 02 have been receiving the rent. In any event, JD no. 01 chose not to appear in the main case to contest and now the decree has attained finality. Even otherwise, no any other legal impediment seems to hinder the way of execution of the same.  
7.	With this observation, therefore, the instant Execution Application is allowed and the mode of execution proposed by the decree-holder is taken into effect.
8.	Quintessentially, before issuing the final decree on the same day, a preliminary decree should have been issued for ascertaining the quantum and period of calculation of the rent, but unfortunately the needful was not done. Nonetheless, once again, the dictates given under Section 47, CPC are referred to for fair and complete satisfaction of the subject decree. Accordingly, the application under consideration is allowed in the following terms:
The Nazir of this Court is directed to visit the suit property, ascertain the rent of the suit property since 01-09-2020 till date by inquiring into the rents of similar properties in the vicinity of suit property, calculate the same and submit the report accordingly within 30 days hereof. 
The Nazir is also to inquire and submit report regarding the tenant who is in possession of the suit property and any contract to the same effect that is in his possession and submit such report. 
The decree-holders are directed to furnish the schedule of any other property in the name of judgment-debtors 01 and 02 or his legal representatives wherefrom the decree may be satisfied, within the period of 30 days hereof.
Announced in open Court. 
Given under my hand and Seal of the Court this 08th day of March, 2025



(AMBREEN BATOOL FATIMA)

	This is a Suit for Recovery of Rs. 75,522/- along with cost of funds, U/s 9 of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001, filed by the Plaintiff Bank against the defendant named above. 
	The brief facts as narrated in the plaint are that the Plaintiff is a Banking Company, having Principal Office at Karachi and is also engaged in providing loan facilities to its Customers. Whereas, the defendants are  the Customers of the Plaintiff Bank, within the meaning of Section 2(c) of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001.  
It is asserted in the Plaint that on 05.09.2012 defendant No. 1 had requested to obtain one Unit Suzuki Cultus VXR E-II, Model 2012 by virtue of Ijarah Lease Facility.  The Plaintiff Bank on the said request of defendant No. 1, issued said finance facility, whereby they offered Ijarah Facility with unit price/lease amount of Rs.9,90,000/-.  The defendant No. 1 duly signed the said application form and offer letter as his token of acknowledgment. 
It is further asserted in the Plaint that the defendant No. 1 entered into Ijarah (Lease) agreement with the Plaintiff Bank, whereby the vehicle was financed by the Plaintiff Bank to the defendant No. 1 on certain terms and conditions of the said agreement, which were accepted by the defendant no.1. To further secure the above finance, the defendant no.2 executed his personal guarantee in favor of the Plaintiff. 
It is alleged in the plaint that the defendant no.1, despite fully utilizing the said finance facility, failed to pay back the outstanding amount as per agreed terms and conditions and committed default in fulfilling his financial and contractual obligations. According to the plaint, a sum of Rs. 75,522/- is due and payable by the defendant to the Plaintiff. The breakup of amount claimed by the Plaintiff, is reproduced as under:

Due to the above circumstances, the Plaintiff has filed the present suit with following prayer:    
A Decree may graciously be passed in favour of the Plaintiff Bank and against defendants for a total sum of Rs. 75,522/- being the outstanding principal and rental. 

The decretal amount be ordered to be realized by execution of personal decree against the defendants.

Pass an order for attachment, repossession and sale of the leased assets namely Suzuki Cultus E-II bearing Registration No. LEE-12-9823, Engine No. F571647 Chassis No. 478523 in favour of the Plaintiff Bank. 

The Suit of the Plaintiff be decreed with costs and cost of funds alongwith all expenses incurred and / or to be incurred by the Plaintiff Bank during the pendency of the Suit. 

Any other relief which this Hon’ble Court deems fit and proper may also be awarded.

After admission of the suit, summonses were issued against the defendants at their addresses given in the plaint, through all prescribed modes of service. The summonses were also published in daily newspapers Nawa-e-Waqt, Karachi, and The News, Karachi, in their issues dated 02.10.2024. But, the defendants failed to submit any application seeking leave to defend themselves in this case, during the stipulated period of 30 days. Hence, the present suit was ordered to be proceeded as ex-parte against them.
I have heard the learned counsel for the Plaintiff Bank, who has explained the breakup of accounts and argued upon this suit, at large. He has also produced all the relevant original documents before this Court, which were seen and returned.  
A perusal of the Statement of Accounts and breakup of the liabilities for said Finance Facility extended by the Plaintiff Bank, reveals that the same has not been certified as per the provisions of Bankers’ Books Evidence, Act 1891, as per Section 2(8) of the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891. Hence, the said Statement of Accounts is not a certified copy, as per the provisions of law and the compliance of Section 9(2) of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001, has not been made, which is mandatory in nature. On this point, I would rely upon the case law of Appollo Textile Mills versus Soneri Bank Ltd. Reported in 2012 CLD 337 S.C, wherein it was observed as under:
“Subsection (2) of Section 9 of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001, makes it mandatory for a Banking Institution to support its plaint in a suit against the customer by a Statement of Accounts duly certified under the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 and also by all other relevant documents relating to grant of finance.  Without such a Statement of Accounts filed along with the plaint, a customer will obviously remain totally unaware of the amount advanced, markup charged and the basis, breakup, premise mode of calculation of account, nature of default and the actual amount of bank’s claim against the defendant customer.  He will thus be unable to frame his defence within the limited period prescribed by law, to show reasonable, serious and plausible grounds of contest to be able to seek and obtain leave to defend the suit. Absence of filing the requisite statements of accounts along with the plaint, will essentially amount to absence of providing adequate, proper and reasonable opportunity of defence to the defending customer.  Being thus unable to file a proper leave petition within thirty days under section 10 (2) or within 21 days under section 10 (12) of the Ordinance, such a customer may or may not later be able to amend his leave petition. His defence shall thus be rendered illusory, hence denied.  Upon the compliance a Banking Company with the provisions of Section 9 (2) of the Ordinance, depends the right of the defense of a defendant in the summary suits as visualized under the Ordinance, where for, the filing of duly certified statements of the accounts by a Banking Company along with its plaint, cannot be taken to be a mere formality or technicality. This provision can only be held to be mandatory. Without strict compliance where with, the plaint is incomplete and cannot become basis of a suit under this law.  

It was further observed in the above decision: 
“The similarity of the provisions legislated in Section 9 and 10 of the Ordinance leads to identical consequences in the absence of the demanded accounts and the documents. Suit of the Plaintiff institution will be rejectable while defendants’ leave petition will be exposed to rejection etc. A Plaintiff Institution may be rendered unable or deficient in appropriately setting up its answers to the accounts, disputed amounts and facts of the defendant in reply to the leave application as per section 10 (8) of the Ordinance.  And that, in the absence of the requisite account and the facts etc. in defense filed by a defendant in the leave petition, a plaintiff will remain unaware of the admitted or denied or disputed accounts and facts of the defendants, to adequately, seriously and reasonably pursue the suit and its trial.  This will obviously defeat the intent and object of the provided provisions of the Financial Institutions, (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001.

In the absence of the support of statements of accounts and finance documents, Bank’s plaint was liable to be rejected.  

 The upshot of my above discussion is that the present suit is not maintainable and barred by the law of Limitation. So also, the mandatory provision of Section 9 (2) of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001, has not been complied with by the Plaintiff Bank. I, therefore, dismiss this suit, with no order as to costs. Let the decree be prepared by the office, accordingly.

(Defendants)SUIT FOR PERMANENT INJUNCTION Present:	Learned counsel for the parties. JUDGMENT:		Brief facts of this suit as per plaint are that plaintiff No.1 and predecessor in interest of plaintiffs No.2 to 5 namely Mushtaq Ahmed purchased the suit house shops from defendant vide registered sale deed No.2338 dated 13.07.2012 with specific meats and bounds; that now defendant wants to interfere into the possession of plaintiff and to close the passage, change the nature of suit property. Plaintiff repeatedly asked the defendant not to so but they refused, hence, this suit.  2.		Defendant contested the suit through filing written statements/written reply, wherein he raised certain preliminary as well legal objection and prayed for dismissal of this suit.  		Out of the divergent pleadings of the parties following issues were framed by my learned predecessor on 07.12.2020;ISSUES: 1.	Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get decree for permanent 	injunction as prayed for in the plaint? OPP2.	Whether suit of the plaintiffs is not maintainable in its 	presence form? OPD3.	Whether plaintiffs have no cause of action to file this suit? 	OPD4.	Whether suit of the plaintiffs is false and frivolous and liable 	to dismissed with special costs u/s 35-A of CPC? OPD  5.	Relief. 		After framing of issues parties were directed to produce their respective evidence.3.		In oral evidence, plaintiff No.2(being special attorney of plaintiffs No.1,3 & 5) appeared as PW.1(he produced special power of attorney as Exh.P1) alongwith Syed Anees Ali Shah and Shahid Iqbal as PW.2 & PW.3 respectively. In documentary evidence, they produced attested copy of registered sale deed No.2338 and concluded their oral as well as documentary evidence. 4.		On the other hand, defendant himself appeared as DW.1. In documentary evidence, defendant produced attested copies of registered sale deeds as Exh.D2 & Exh.D3 and concluded his oral as well as documentary evidence. 5.		 Arguments heard. Record perused.6.		My issue wise findings are as under;ISSUE No.1. 7.		 Onus to prove this issue was placed upon the plaintiffs. In this regard, the plaintiff No.2(being special attorney of plaintiffs No.1,3,4 & 5) while appearing as PW-1 and deposed that they are owner in possession of suit shops through registered sale deed No.2338 dated 13.07.2012 and defendant has no concern with the suit shops but he wants to interfere into the possession of plaintiff and block the passage of plaintiffs without any legal justification. However, during cross-examination, PW.1 deposed that he is using the shops as per meets and bounds mentioned in registered sale deed Exh.P2 and there is no nowhere mention of stairs in the registered sale deed. He admitted during cross-examination that according to registered sale deed, defendant is not closing his passage. He also admitted that defendant never tried to break the door of shop for illegal entrance. 8.		In order to prove their stance, plaintiffs also produced Syed Anees Ali Shah and Shahid Iqbal as PW.2 & PW.3 respectively. They were cross-examined by the learned counsel for the defendant and during cross-examination, they specifically admitted that according to registered sale deed Exh.P2, defendant never tried to dispossess the plaintiffs from suit shops. They also admitted that defendant did not try to occupy the suit shop owned and possessed by the plaintiff. To strengthen the stance of plaintiffs, they also produced registered sale deed Exh.P2, which was perused, wherein in fact there is no mention regarding ownership of stairs. The main stance of the plaintiffs is that they are owners in possession of suit shop according to registered sale deed Exh.P2 and defendant is trying to interfere into his possession. During cross-examination PWs have admitted that defendant is not interfering into the possession of plaintiffs as alleged by them. This fact has also admitted by the defendant in his written statement as well as during evidence. Learned counsel for the plaintiff cross-examined the DWs at length but they did not depose a single word in favour of plaintiffs. In accordance with the principle laid down in case of “Haji Muhammad Hussain Vs. Muhammad Abbas” (2001 YLR 1767), where is was held that:“A suit for permanent injunction is maintainable only when there is a credible threat of interfere with possession, the court finds that plaintiff has failed to demonstrate any such threat in the case”.9.		Plaintiff’s acknowledgment that defendant has not interfere with the possession further supports the conclusion that there is no basis for the relief sought. Moreover, as per ruling in Fazal Din Vs. Muhammad Jan (2013 LHC 4872), it is established that admissions made during cross-examination are binding and can significantly effect the outcome of the case. In present case, PWs negate the necessity for an injunction, as there is no ongoing interference to grant such relief. In the light of above discussion, plaintiffs have miserably failed to prove their claim through cogent, convincing and confidence inspiring evidence therefore, this issue is decided against the plaintiffs.ISSUES No.2 & 3:       10.		Onus probandi of both issues were placed upon the defendants as the plaintiff has badly failed to prove issue No.1 through cogent and reliable evidence, hence, in the light of my findings on issue No.1, both issue are hereby disposed off accordingly. RELIEF.11.		Keeping in view of my issue wise findings, suit of the plaintiff is hereby dismissed. No order as to costs. Decree sheet be prepared accordingly.
